newsitem.title: UK: Non-oil commodities are dull, weaken in some markets.
newsitem.headline: Non-oil commodities are dull, weaken in some markets.

text.p: Oil which hit a new post-Gulf War record that took it above $25 per barrel on Tuesday again eclipsed other commodity markets where prices were little changed or lower.
Palladium sank to the lowest since 1993 and European wheat futures also retreated. Gold was hardly changed and another bid by copper to make a rally fizzled out.
Speculative money again showed scant interest in the commodities away from crude oil.
London November futures for the benchmark North Sea Brent blend crude broke above $25 a barrel for the first time since the 1990/1991 Gulf War. But they eased later.
Brent has shot up by $7 a barrel since mid-June, driven by concern over tensions in the Middle East and persistently low stocks of heating fuel in pre-winter Western markets.

Copper prices ended barely changed after a new move toward strong technical resistance at $1,970 per tonne failed and they were unchanged around $1,935 late in the London Metal Exchange (LME) afternoon.
But aluminium managed to edge up, supported by physical demand in Asia, away from recent 2 1/2-year lows, to end $30 per tonne firmer at $1,356.
Gold was little changed at a London close of $381.45 an ounce but palladium fixed in London at $116.25, the lowest setting since September 14, 1993.
A low bid was quoted at $115.75.
Prices of the white metal, used primarily in electronics, catalytic converters and dentistry, have been declining steadily since rallying to a high of around $175 an ounce in April 1995.
Dealers attributed a slide in recent months to steady sales from key producer Russia and slack demand from the Japanese electronics industry.
Lead prices may be vulnerable later this week in reaction to an estimate of a 1997 surplus available late Tuesday.
World refined output of lead next year is estimated rising to 5.92 million tonnes, exceeding consumption of 5.86 million, the International Lead and Zinc Study Group (ILZSG) said.
London wheat futures extened a slide that reflects a bumper European harvest.

A strong pound sterling and bumper harvest put new pressure on London International Financial Futures Exchange grain futures generally with wheat as much as 1.40 sterling a tonne down at one point. A new contract low of 97.40 sterling was paid for November.
An estimate by French cereals analyst Strategie Grains raised this year's European Union cereals harvest forecast by 2.5 million tonnes to a record 201.4 million.
But Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) December wheat futures were little changed just above $4.25 per bushel.
